c.tagline: Guangdong's inkstone capital, where karst peaks rise from Star Lake beside a Ming Dynasty city wall.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered with a base fare around ¥8-10 for the first 2-3km; the DiDi app is more convenient than street-hailing for non-Chinese speakers and lets you set a destination in advance.

emergency.note: China does not use a single unified emergency number; 110 reaches police, 120 reaches ambulance services, and 119 reaches fire.

hoods: Star Lake / Seven Star Crags Area
hood_desc: The scenic core of Zhaoqing around Star Lake and the Seven Star Crags, an AAAAA-rated karst-peak park often compared to Guilin; best for travelers who want the city's signature natural landmark right outside their hotel.
The historic quarter in and around Zhaoqing's Ming Dynasty city wall, with the Chongxi Pagoda, old temples, and traditional streets; suits travelers wanting a slower-paced, heritage-focused base.
The commercial heart of Duanzhou District along Tianning Road, with malls, restaurants, and everyday city life; practical for travelers who want easy transit and shopping access.

A green, spread-out district built around Dinghu Mountain, China's first nature reserve, with hot springs and forest trails; ideal for travelers prioritizing nature and relaxation over sightseeing density.

A quieter northern residential district away from the main tourist core, offering a more local, lower-key look at everyday Zhaoqing; suited to travelers who prefer calm surroundings with easy bus access downtown.

water.note: Stick to bottled or boiled water; tap water is not potable.

transit.hours: City buses generally run about 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM; no metro or dedicated night bus network.
transit.pay: Fares (¥2-4) are paid in cash on board or via mobile QR code (Alipay/WeChat Pay); no dedicated rechargeable transit card is required for visitors.
transit.note: Zhaoqing has no metro; buses, DiDi ride-hailing, and taxis cover the city, while the Guangzhou-Zhaoqing Intercity Railway and Zhaoqing East high-speed rail station connect to the wider Greater Bay Area.

bus: Intercity coaches to Guangzhou, Shenzhen, and Hong Kong

car.idp: Not recognized; a Chinese driver's license or certified translation is required

Airport shuttle plus Guangzhou-Zhaoqing Intercity Railway (~2 hrs total)

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in mainland China and is not expected at restaurants, taxis, or hotels.

food.desc: A prized local carp raised in Zhaoqing's ponds, usually steamed whole with light soy so the sweet, fine flesh stays intact.

landmarks: Seven Star Crags (Qixingyan)
Seven limestone crags arranged like the Big Dipper rise from willow-fringed lakes, laced with arched bridges, grottoes and cliff inscriptions.
Star Lake Wetlands
Boardwalks and pleasure boats cross the lake system wrapping the crags, where flocks of cranes wheel overhead in daily flying displays.
Zhaoqing Ancient City Wall
A remarkably complete Song-dynasty wall still circles the old town; walk its ramparts to the rebuilt Piyun Tower.
Dinghu Mountain
China's first nature reserve, a UNESCO biosphere of subtropical forest, waterfalls and emerald pools an easy ride from downtown.
Qingyun Temple
A 17th-century Buddhist monastery folded into Dinghu Mountain's forested slopes, famed for its thousand-person wok and vegetarian cuisine.
Meian (Plum Monastery)
A monastery founded in 996 AD honoring Zen's Sixth Patriarch Huineng, who is said to have planted plum trees here.
Yuejiang Tower
A stately Ming tower above the Xi River, counted among southern China's famous towers and housing the Ye Ting Independent Regiment memorial.
Chongxi Pagoda
A slender nine-story Ming pagoda mirrored in the Xi River, among the tallest of its kind in Guangdong and lovely at dusk.
Licha Bagua Village
An extraordinary Ming-era village laid out as a feng shui octagram, its dizzying concentric lanes best appreciated from the viewing tower.
China Inkstone Culture Village (Baishi)
The home of Duan inkstones, China's most prized, where workshops still carve purple stone quarried nearby since the Tang dynasty.

train.note: There are no cross-border trains from Zhaoqing; Hong Kong and Macau are reached by coach or by changing onto a Hong Kong-bound high-speed train. Zhaoqing East is the high-speed station on the Guangzhou-Nanning line, with Guangzhou South about 40 minutes away and onward connections across southern China, while Zhaoqing station is served by the Guangzhou-Zhaoqing intercity railway and by conventional trains on the Sanmao line. The old KCR through train that once linked Zhaoqing directly with Hong Kong's Hung Hom no longer operates, so for Hong Kong change at Guangzhou South for a West Kowloon service. All tickets go through 12306 with your passport.

intl.op: cross-boundary coaches from Zhaoqing's city bus terminals — tickets at the terminal counter or through local agents; no official English booking site

bus.note: Cross-boundary coaches to Hong Kong and Macau use dedicated terminals in Zhaoqing and take roughly 4-5 hours to Hong Kong, with immigration handled at the Shenzhen or Zhuhai land border en route - carry your passport and any required Chinese visa for re-entry. Domestic buses from Guangzhou run very frequently from several departure points and take about two hours, and there are direct coaches from Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport, which is often the simplest way in. There are also regular services to Kaiping for the diaolou watchtowers. Within Zhaoqing, 32 public bus routes plus two sightseeing routes cover the city and Seven Star Crags.

ferry.note: Zhaoqing sits on the Xi (West) River, and Hong Kong's Chu Kong Passenger Transport historically ran an express catamaran down to Hong Kong, but no such sailing is currently sold on the operator's site (https://www.cksp.com.hk/) and the river now carries freight rather than scheduled passengers. The boats you will actually find are the sightseeing craft on Star Lake and short cruises through the Seven Star Crags.
